..
As of 430 AM Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... Showers and thunderstorms and rain-cooled air this 
afternoon will provide localized relief from continued heat 
highlighted by a Heat Advisory that remains in effect today for the 
srn Piedmont, Sandhills, and srn and cntl Coastal Plain. 

Cyclonic, nwly flow aloft will prevail across the OH Valley and 
middle Atlantic, between a slow-moving cyclone over the Canadian 
Maritimes and a weakening/collapsing sub-tropical ridge over the srn 
Appalachians. Within that nwly flow regime, a shortwave impulse now 
over nrn IN/wrn Lwr MI, and embedded or slightly preceding MCV/MCS 
over nwrn OH, will progress sewd and across the Virginias today and 
nrn and nern NC through this evening. Weakly falling heights and 
cooling through the mid-levels will result over cntl NC through 12Z 
Sun. Some mesoscale enhanced/acceleration may also result within a 
belt of otherwise 15-25 kts of mid-level northwesterlies over cntl 
and nern NC later this afternoon-evening. 

At the surface, a synoptic front stretched from near the ongoing MCS 
from nrn IN and nwrn OH, esewd across wrn PA and s-cntl NJ. This 
boundary will progress only slowly swwd and across the Virginias 
tonight and into cntl NC early Sun. The front will be preceded by 
both a pre-frontal trough and outflow segments stretching 
discontinuously from Friday's convection over cntl/ern NC nwwd to 
the aforementioned MCS (and developing strong cold pool) that will 
propagate away from the synoptic front through the morning and 
possibly into the nrn Piedmont of NC by midday-early afternoon. 

Each of the the surface boundaries noted above will serve as 
possible foci for renewed convective development and/or diurnal 
intensification of upstream convection, with strong daytime heating 
into the 90s F once again. The most likely scenario will be for 
initially widely scattered pulse/multi-cells to develop in-situ over 
cntl NC along the pre-frontal trough at about the same time that the 
upstream convection and outflow (and probably some degree of an 
ongoing MCS), are expected to move into the nrn Piedmont. However, 
it remains unclear if and how quickly that upstream MCS may 
intensify over parts of cntl NC, given that instability will be 
comparatively weaker over the nrn Piedmont versus the Sandhills and 
srn/cntl Coastal Plain, owing to lower mean mixing ratios/surface 
dewpoints there; and it may arrive there prior to peak diurnal 
heating. And by the time it reaches the richer low-level moisture 
and initially greater instability across srn zones, those areas may 
have already been locally cooled and stabilized by convection that 
may have developed in-situ along the pre-frontal trough. Damaging 
wind gusts will pose the primary risk regardless, with that risk 
greatest along sewd-propagating multicell clusters. Some transient 
supercells and a risk for hail will be possible over the ne Piedmont 
and nrn Coastal Plain, where effective shear will be locally 
maximized immediately swd/swwd of the track of the MCV, and where 
surface winds will probably have some nly component (and elongation 
of hodographs in the lowest kilometer) poleward of the pre-frontal 
trough and outflow. 

It will otherwise remain dangerously hot today, especially across 
srn zones that were not overturned and diabatically-cooled by 
Friday's convection; and no changes were made to the Heat Advisory 
that remains in effect there from 11A to 8P.


KEY MESSAGE 2... After the passage of the cold front by Sunday 
morning, a shortwave trough may bring continued shower chances on 
Sunday, then somewhat cooler and drier air will filter into central 
NC. 

The cold front should be south of the region by Sunday morning.
However, model guidance is suggesting that some moisture will linger 
in the region through the day on Sunday. Additionally, it appears 
that a weak shortwave trough may move through the region sometime on 
Sunday. This could allow for post-frontal rain to linger through the 
day. Overall light rain showers are expected as minimal instability 
should be in place in the post frontal regime, however a few rumbles 
of thunder cannot be ruled out. 

High temperatures should return to the 80s from Sunday through 
Tuesday or Wednesday, before returning to the 90s by mid-to-late 
week. The chance of rain during this period will be generally low 
each day, with an isolated diurnal thunderstorm possible each 
afternoon/evening especially late week as warming is occurring and 
moisture is returning to the region. It looks like another cold 
front may pass through central NC sometime late week, however 
details are still uncertain.
